Order:

(Per Hon'ble Sri Justice K. Lakshman) Heard Mr. Mohammed Aslam, learned counsel for the petitioner and learned Special Government Pleader representing learned Additional Advocate General appearing on behalf of the respondents.

2. This writ petition is filed to issue a writ of habeas corpus directing the respondents to produce the detenue viz.,, Syeda Uzma Fathima W/o Mohd. Ali, now detained in Central Prison, Chanchalguda,
Hyderabad, and to order her release forthwith by setting aside the detention order dated 03.06.2023 passed by respondent No.4 and the consequential approval order dated 08.06.2023 passed by respondent No.3 vide G.O.Rt.No.833 declaring them as illegal.
3. Respondent No.4 passed the detention order dated 03.06.2023 against the detenue under the provisions of Section - 3 (2) of the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Boot-leggers,
KL,J & SKS,J Dacoits, Drug-Offenders, Goondas, Immoral Traffic Offenders Land- Grabbers,
Spurious Seed Offenders, Insecticide Offenders, Fertiliser Offenders, Food Adulteration Offenders,
Fake Document Offenders, Scheduled Commodities Offenders, Forest Offenders, Gaming Offenders,
Sexual Offenders, Explosive Substances Offenders, Arms Offenders, Cyber Crime Offenders and White Collar or Financial Offenders Act, 1986 (Act No.1 of 1986) (for short 'Act No.1 of 1986'), under the category of 'Dacoit' as defined under Section - 2 (c) of the Act No.1 of 1986.
4.

The impugned detention order was passed by respondent No.4 - detaining authority relying on the following two (02) crimes:

5. Crime No.32 of 2023 was registered by Musheerabad Police Station against the detenue for the offences punishable under Sections KL,J & SKS,J - 395, 419, 387 and 120B of IPC and Section - 25 (1) (A) of the Indian Arms Act.
After completion of investigation, the Investigating Officer laid the charge sheet and the same is pending for committal.
The detenue is arraigned as accused No.5 in the said crime.
6. Crime No.6 of 2023 was registered by Santosh Nagar Police Station for the offences punishable under Sections - 395 and 384 read with 34 of IPC.
On completion of investigation, the Investigating Officer laid the charge sheet and the same is pending for committal.

In this crime also, the detenue is arraigned as accused No.5.
7.
Mr. Mohd. Aslam, learned counsel for the petitioner, would submit that the impugned detention order was issued without application of mind.
The detaining authority did not consider the material properly.
Therefore, there is no subjective satisfaction by the detaining authority while issuing the impugned detention order.
Thus, the detention order and the consequential approval order are liable to be set aside.

8. On the other hand, learned Special Government Pleader representing learned Additional Advocate General would submit that the allegations levelled against the detenue are serious and dangerous KL,J & SKS,J in nature and she is a habitual and dangerous offender involved in the above crimes.

The detaining authority, considering the entire material available on record and after arriving at the subjective satisfaction only passed the detention order in order to prevent the detenue from committing similar offences and the same was approved by respondent No.3.
There is no error in it.

i) He has also placed reliance on the principle laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Vijay Kumar v. Union of India 1 and Smt. K. Aruna Kumari v. Government of Andhra Pradesh 2.
9.

Perusal of detention order, dated 03.06.2023, passed by respondent No.4 would reveal that the detenue along with her associates target the business/vulnerable people, bait them and trap them by taking photographs (selfies) with the victims and blackmail them threatening the victims to make the photos public and also with dire consequences at the point of knives and extort money from Syed Abdul Masi vs The State Of Telangana on 1 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/29683246/
2 them to earn easy and illegal money to lead a lavish life.

sentences.text: It is also mentioned that the aforesaid crimes would amply demonstrate the habitual nature of committing crime and creating large scale fear and panic among the people adversely affecting the maintenance of .
(1988) 1 SCC 296 KL,J & SKS,J 'public order'.
The detenue voluntarily confessed to have committed the aforesaid offences.

Thus, the detaining authority having considered the entire material on record arrived at the subjective satisfaction that the detenue has been habitually committing dacoities and dangerous offences by trapping the victims in the honey-trap along with her associates in an organized manner in the limits of different police stations of Hyderabad Police Commissionerate and, therefore, she is a 'dacoit' as defined in Clause (c) of Section - 2 of the Act No.1 of 1986.

Thus,
with a view to prevent the detenue from acting in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of 'public order' respondent No.4 - detaining authority passed the impugned detention order dated 03.06.2023 and the same was approved by respondent No.3 vide G.O.Rt.No.833 of General Administration (Spl. Law & Order) Department, dated 08.06.2023.
Thus, according to the respondents, the case of the detenue falls under the category of 'Dacoit'.

10. Section - 2 (c) of the Act No.1 of Act, 1986 defines "dacoit" which means a person who either by himself or as a member of or leader of a gang commits or abets the commission of any of the KL,J &
SKS,J offences punishable under sections 395 to 400 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
11.

While passing the detention order, the detaining authority not only considered the modus operandi of the detenue in commission of offences, but also considered the allegations levelled against the detenue which are grave and serious in nature.
Therefore, in order to prevent the detenue from committing similar offences passed the impugned detention order.
12. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Ashok Kumar v. Delhi Administration 3 observed that preventive detention is devised to afford protection to society.
The object is not to punish a man for having done something but to intercept before he does it and to prevent him from doing.

13. In Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar 4, the Apex Court held as under:
"...Does the expression "public order" take in every kind of disorder or only some?

entities.text: Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar 4
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The answer to this serves to distinguish "public order" from "law and order" because the latter undoubtedly takes in all of them.
Public order if disturbed, must lead to public disorder.
Every breach of .
AIR 1966 SC 740 KL,J & SKS,J the peace does not lead to public disorder.
When two drunkards quarrel and fight there is disorder but not public disorder.
They can be dealt with under the powers to maintain law and order but cannot be detained on the ground that they were disturbing public order.
Suppose that the two fighters were of rival communities and one of them tried to raise communal passions.
The problem is still one of law and order but it raises the apprehension of public disorder.
Other examples can be imagined.
The contravention of law always affects order but before it can be said to affect public order, it must affect the community or the public at large.

A mere disturbance of law and order leading to disorder is thus not necessarily sufficient for action under the Defence of India Act but disturbances which subvert the public Syed Abdul Masi vs The State Of Telangana on 1 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/29683246/
3 order are.

entities.text: public Syed Abdul Masi vs The State Of Telangana
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: A District Magistrate is entitled to take action under Rule 30(1)(b) to prevent subversion of public order but not in aid of maintenance of law and order under ordinary circumstances.

It will thus appear that just as "public order" in the rulings of this Court (earlier cited) was said to comprehend disorders of less gravity than those affecting "security of State", "law and order" also comprehends disorders of less gravity than those affecting public order".
One has to imagine three concentric circles.
Law and order represents the largest circle within which is the next circle representing public order and the smallest circle represents security of State.

It is then easy to see that an act may affect law and order but not public order just as an act may affect public order but not security of the State."
14.
In Vijay Narain Singh v. State of Bihar 5, a three Judge Bench of the Apex Court had an occasion to deal with the expression .

entities.text: Vijay Narain Singh v. State of Bihar 5
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: (1984) 3 SCC 14 KL,J & SKS,J 'habitually'

and held that the expression 'habitually' would mean 'repeatedly' or 'persistently' implying a thread of continuity, stringing together similar repetitive acts, and a single act or omission would not characterize as an act of 'habitual'.

The Apex Court was of the opinion that to qualify as a 'habit', a person must have grown accustomed to leading a life of crime, whereby it would be a force of habit, inherent or latent, in an individual with a criminal instinct, with a criminal disposition of mind, that makes him as dangerous to society in general.

15. As discussed above, in Crime No.32 of 2023, the detenue along with her associates looted an amount of Rs.5,05,000/- from the complainant therein, while an amount of Rs.47,000/- from the complainant in Crime No.6 of 2023 under the guise of dating and giving catering order respectively.
The allegations levelled against the detenue are serious and grave in nature.

Thus, the detaining authority while invoking the powers under the Act No.1 of 1986, has to consider the entire material on record and come to a subjective satisfaction that due to the acts committed by the detenue,
nature of offences and the manner in which the same were committed would disturb the public order.
To prevent the detenue from committing the KL,J & SKS,J similar offences, the detaining authority shall issue preventive detention order against the detenue.
The Apex Court, this Court has to consider facts and circumstances of each case on case to case basis.
16. There is no dispute with regard to the legal proposition that the detention order shall be issued in rarest of rare cases, that too, to prevent the detenue from committing similar offences.
Article - 21 of the Constitution of India enshrined the detenue the fundamental right of personal liberty which is precious right enshrined to the citizens as per the Constitution of India.
At the same time, duty cast upon the 'State' as defined under Article - 12 of the Constitution of India to maintain law and order as well as public order.
When there is disturbance to the public order, it is the duty of the 'State' to invoke the procedure laid down under the Act No.1 of 1986, to prevent the detenue from committing similar offences.

17. As discussed above, the facts of the present case would reveal that the detenue is having criminal history and the allegations levelled against her in the aforesaid two (02) crimes are serious and grave in nature.

Certainly, the acts of the detenue in commission of the aforesaid offences disturb the 'public order' and the impact of the KL,J & SKS,J said offences would create panic in the minds Syed Abdul Masi vs The State Of Telangana on 1 September, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/29683246/
4 of the public.

sentences.text: The detaining authority having considered all the said aspects arrived at the subjective satisfaction and passed the impugned detention order.

Therefore, viewed from any angle, we are of the considered view that there is no error in the impugned detention order dated 03.06.2023 passed by respondent No.4 and the consequential approval order dated 08.06.2023 passed by respondent No.3.
Thus, the writ petition fails and the same is liable to be dismissed.
18. The present writ petition is accordingly dismissed.
In the circumstances of the cases, there shall be no order as to costs.
As a sequel, the miscellaneous petitions, if any, pending in the writ petition shall stand closed.
